claim: IFT trains are multimegadalton assemblies of IFT proteins and motors that traffic proteins in cilia.
source: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) trains, multimegadalton assemblies of IFT proteins and motors, traffic proteins in cilia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational description of IFT trains.

claim: IFT-A and motor proteins are recruited from the cell body to the basal body pool, assembled into trains, move through the cilium, and disperse back into the cell body.
source: IFT-A and motor proteins are recruited from the cell body to the basal body pool, assembled into trains, move through the cilium, and disperse back into the cell body.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the experimental observations.

claim: IFT-B proteins from retrograde trains reenter the pool and a portion is reused directly in anterograde trains indicating a 'semi-open' system.
source: In contrast to this 'open' system, IFT-B proteins from retrograde trains reenter the pool and a portion is reused directly in anterograde trains indicating a 'semi-open' system.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Similar IFT systems were observed in Tetrahymena thermophila and IMCD3 cells.
source: Similar IFT systems were also observed in Tetrahymena thermophila and IMCD3 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from experiments in these organisms.

claim: FRAP analysis indicated that IFT proteins and motors of a given train are sequentially recruited to the basal bodies.
source: FRAP analysis indicated that IFT proteins and motors of a given train are sequentially recruited to the basal bodies.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on FRAP experiments.

claim: IFT dynein and tubulin cargoes are loaded briefly before the trains depart.
source: IFT dynein and tubulin cargoes are loaded briefly before the trains depart.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: The pool contains IFT trains in multiple stages of assembly queuing for successive release into the cilium upon completion.
source: We conclude that the pool contains IFT trains in multiple stages of assembly queuing for successive release into the cilium upon completion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract based on all experimental findings.

claim: The assembly of most cilia and flagella depends on bidirectional intraflagellar transport (IFT).
source: The assembly of most cilia and flagella (terms used interchangeably) depends on bidirectional intraflagellar transport (IFT) (Rosenbaum and Witman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosenbaum and Witman, 2002.

claim: Anterograde IFT trains move from the ciliary base to the tip powered by kinesin-2.
source: Anterograde IFT trains move from the ciliary base to the tip powered by kinesin-2
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In retrograde IFT, the trains return to the cell body employing IFT dynein.
source: in retrograde IFT, the trains return to the cell body employing IFT dynein.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: IFT trains transport proteins in and out of cilia to support ciliary assembly, maintenance, and signaling.
source: The IFT trains transport proteins in and out of cilia to support ciliary assembly, maintenance, and signaling (for review: [Lechtreck, 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review by Lechtreck, 2015.

claim: IFT trains are composed of IFT motors and IFT particles.
source: They are composed of IFT motors and IFT particles
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: IFT particles consist of 22 conserved IFT proteins organized into biochemically stable IFT-A, IFT-B1 and IFT-B2 subcomplexes each consisting of equimolar amounts of 6, 10 and 6 proteins, respectively.
source: the latter consisting of 22 conserved IFT proteins organized into biochemically stable IFT-A, IFT-B1 and IFT-B2 subcomplexes each consisting of equimolar amounts of 6, 10 and 6 proteins, respectively (Cole et al., 1998; Katoh et al., 2016; Taschner et al., 2012, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Cole et al., 1998; Katoh et al., 2016; Taschner et al., 2012, 2016).

claim: At the ultrastructural level, the trains possess a periodic substructure presumably resulting from the 22-subunit IFT particles.
source: At the ultrastructural level, the trains possess a periodic substructure presumably resulting from the 22-subunit IFT particles (Pigino et al., 2009; Stepanek and Pigino, 2016; Vannuccini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Pigino et al., 2009; Stepanek and Pigino, 2016; Vannuccini et al., 2016) and includes speculative reasoning ('presumably').

claim: Numerous protein-protein interactions within the IFT particle have been identified.
source: Numerous protein-protein interactions within the IFT particle have been identified
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: A 15-subunit IFT-B complex has been assembled from recombinant proteins.
source: a 15-subunit IFT-B complex has been assembled from recombinant proteins (Hirano et al., 2017; Taschner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Hirano et al., 2017; Taschner et al., 2016).

claim: The oligomerization of purified IFT complexes to the size of trains observed in vivo under cell free conditions has not yet been reported.
source: The oligomerization of purified IFT complexes to the size of trains observed in vivo under cell free conditions has not yet been reported.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Western blot analyses showed that 90% or more of the IFT proteins reside in the cell body.
source: Western blot analyses showed that 90% or more of the IFT proteins reside in the cell body, a portion of which is concentrated around the basal bodies forming an IFT pool (Ahmed et al., 2008; Deane et al., 2001; Richey and Qin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ahmed et al., 2008; Deane et al., 2001; Richey and Qin, 2012).

claim: A portion of IFT proteins is concentrated around the basal bodies forming an IFT pool.
source: Western blot analyses showed that 90% or more of the IFT proteins reside in the cell body, a portion of which is concentrated around the basal bodies forming an IFT pool (Ahmed et al., 2008; Deane et al., 2001; Richey and Qin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ahmed et al., 2008; Deane et al., 2001; Richey and Qin, 2012).

claim: The IFT trains emerge from the basal body pool and enter the cilia in a kinesin-2 dependent manner.
source: The IFT trains emerge from the basal body pool (bb-pool) and enter the cilia in a kinesin-2 dependent manner (Kozminski et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Kozminski et al., 1995).

claim: The IFT bb-pool appears to be amorphous at the ultrastructural level.
source: In contrast to the discrete IFT trains observed inside cilia, the IFT bb-pool appears to be amorphous at the ultrastructural level, i.e., bona fide IFT trains with their characteristic zigzag structure are visible only near the distal end of the basal bodies (Rogowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Rogowski et al., 2013).

claim: Bona fide IFT trains with their characteristic zigzag structure are visible only near the distal end of the basal bodies.
source: In contrast to the discrete IFT trains observed inside cilia, the IFT bb-pool appears to be amorphous at the ultrastructural level, i.e., bona fide IFT trains with their characteristic zigzag structure are visible only near the distal end of the basal bodies (Rogowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Rogowski et al., 2013).

claim: IFT-B loss-of-function mutants often fail to assemble cilia presumably due to impaired IFT train formation.
source: IFT-B loss-of-function mutants often fail to assemble cilia presumably due to impaired IFT train formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations and includes speculative reasoning ('presumably').

claim: In IFT-B loss-of-function mutants, the stability of the remaining IFT proteins and their spatial distribution in the bb-pool are altered.
source: In such mutants, the stability of the remaining IFT proteins and their spatial distribution in the bb-pool are altered (see for example: [Hou et al., 2007; Lv et al., 2017; Richey and Qin, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Hou et al., 2007; Lv et al., 2017; Richey and Qin, 2012).

claim: After photobleaching of the bb-pool in Trypanosoma brucei, anterograde traffic of fluorescent IFT trains was transiently interrupted, indicative of bleached trains exiting the bb-pool.
source: After photobleaching of the bb-pool, anterograde traffic of fluorescent IFT trains was transiently interrupted, indicative of bleached trains exiting the bb-pool.
evidence: This is a finding from a study by Buisson et al., 2013 on T. brucei.

claim: In Trypanosoma brucei, the pool signal recovered partially and anterograde IFT traffic resumed albeit with reduced signal strength suggesting that photobleached proteins in the bb-pool mix with unbleached IFT proteins supposedly derived from retrograde trains.
source: The pool signal recovered partially and anterograde IFT traffic resumed albeit with reduced signal strength suggesting that photobleached proteins in the bb-pool mix with unbleached IFT proteins supposedly derived from retrograde trains.
evidence: This is a finding from Buisson et al., 2013 with interpretive reasoning.

claim: A closed IFT system was proposed for Trypanosoma brucei in which the IFT proteins perpetually cycle between the flagellum and the bb-pool with limited exchange of proteins between the flagellum-basal body entity and the rest of the cell body.
source: This led to the proposal of a closed IFT system in which the IFT proteins perpetually cycle between the flagellum and the bb-pool with limited exchange of proteins between the flagellum-basal body entity and the rest of the cell body.
evidence: This is a model proposed by Buisson et al., 2013.

claim: The transgenic strains expressing FP-tagged IFT proteins had normal or nearly normal length flagella.
source: The transgenic strains had normal or nearly normal length flagella
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The transgenic strains expressing FP-tagged IFT proteins displayed IFT traffic with mostly wild-type IFT velocities and anterograde frequencies (~1/s).
source: The transgenic strains had normal or nearly normal length flagella and displayed IFT traffic with mostly wild-type IFT velocities and anterograde frequencies (~1/s)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Retrograde frequencies were more variable in the transgenic strains, which is attributed mostly to the weaker signals of retrograde trains.
source: retrograde frequencies were more variable which we attribute mostly to the weaker signals of retrograde trains (Figure 1A–D; Video 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The various FP-tagged IFT proteins were present in dot-, colon-, or dumbbell-shaped regions near each basal body.
source: The various FP-tagged IFT proteins were present in dot-, colon-, or dumbbell-shaped regions near each basal body
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most FP-tagged IFT proteins showed weak X-shaped signals representing the microtubular flagellar roots.
source: most of them also showed weak X-shaped signals representing the microtubular flagellar roots (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most of KAP-GFP was close to the distal end of the basal bodies followed by accumulations of the tagged IFT-B proteins; the IFT-A proteins and D1bLIC were concentrated deeper in the cell.
source: Focal series from the flagella down into the cell body revealed that most of KAP-GFP was close to the distal end of the basal bodies followed by accumulations of the tagged IFT-B proteins; the IFT-A proteins and D1bLIC were concentrated deeper in the cell (not shown; [Brown et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is based on focal series imaging and supported by a citation (Brown et al., 2015).

claim: The IFT140-sfGFP signals were more peripheral than those of most IFT-B proteins.
source: The IFT140-sfGFP signals were more peripheral than those of most IFT-B proteins.
evidence: This is based on imaging observations.

claim: Different IFT proteins inhabit non-identical spatial domains within the bb-pool.
source: Within the limitations of the technique used, live cell imaging confirms and extends pervious observations on fixed cells indicating that different IFT proteins inhabit non-identical spatial domains within the bb-pool (Hou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on live cell imaging data and supported by a citation (Hou et al., 2007).

claim: The IFT bb-pool signals of all eight FP-tagged IFT particle and motor proteins recovered on average within 3 to 10 s after photobleaching.
source: The IFT bb-pool signals of all eight FP-tagged IFT particle and motor proteins recovered on average within 3 to 10 s (Figure 2B; Video 2).
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2B and Video 2.

claim: Signal recovery typically exceeded 60% of the prebleach strength and often complete recovery to the level of the control bb-pool was observed.
source: Signal recovery typically exceeded 60% of the prebleach strength and often complete recovery to the level of the control bb-pool was observed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative FRAP analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Recovery of the signal was observed after repeated bleaching of the bb-pool indicating that the size of one IFT bb-pool is small as compared to the total cellular supply of IFT proteins.
source: Recovery of the signal was also observed after repeated bleaching of the bb-pool indicating that the size of one IFT bb-pool is small as compared to the total cellular supply of IFT proteins (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on repeated bleaching experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E, with interpretive reasoning.

claim: The KAP-GFP signal recovered in less than 4 s.
source: While the KAP-GFP signal recovered in less than 4 s
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: IFT43-YFP, IFT20-FP and NG-IFT54 required ~9s to reach maximum recovery.
source: IFT43-YFP, IFT20-FP and NG-IFT54 required ~9s to reach maximum recovery (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: IFT proteins in the bb-pool exchange at different rates.
source: In conclusion, IFT proteins in the bb-pool exchange at different rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRAP data showing different recovery times.

claim: For the IFT-B proteins IFT20-NG, IFT46-YFP, and NG-IFT54 the signal intensity of the experimental basal body decreased significantly during FLIP illumination.
source: For the IFT-B proteins IFT20-NG, IFT46-YFP, and NG-IFT54 the signal intensity of the experimental basal body decreased significantly during FLIP illumination (Figure 3C,D,F,G).
evidence: This is based on FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3C,D,F,G.

claim: The fluorescence loss was substantially lower for the tagged IFT27, motor protein subunits, and in particular IFT-A proteins during FLIP illumination.
source: The fluorescence loss was substantially lower for the tagged IFT27, motor protein subunits, and in particular IFT-A proteins (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Video 3).
evidence: This is based on FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3E–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A pronounced fluorescence loss occurred predominately during the first 10–20 s of FLIP.
source: A pronounced fluorescence loss occurred predominately during the first 10–20 s of FLIP
evidence: This is based on FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Some unbleached IFT-B proteins were present in the experimental bb-pool even in prolonged FLIP experiments (>30 s).
source: some unbleached IFT-B proteins were present in the experimental bb-pool even in prolonged FLIP experiments (>30 s; Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on prolonged FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For the NG-IFT54 bb-pool, the plateau was reached after ~15 s (STD 4.4 s, n = 14) of FLIP illumination when the normalized signal strength of the experimental basal body was reduced to ~52% (STD 9.2%, n = 14) of its initial level.
source: For the NG-IFT54 bb-pool, this plateau was reached after ~15 s (STD 4.4 s, n = 14; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) of FLIP illumination when the normalized signal strength of the experimental basal body was reduced to ~52% (STD 9.2%, n = 14; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) of its initial level.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: After switching off the FLIP laser, the basal body signal recovered and retrograde IFT recommenced.
source: After switching off the FLIP laser, the basal body signal recovered and retrograde IFT recommenced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is based on FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Most of IFT27 and the tested IFT-A and motor subunits do not reenter the bb-pool.
source: We conclude that most of IFT27 and the tested IFT-A and motor subunits do not reenter the bb-pool
evidence: This is a conclusion based on FLIP experiments showing minimal fluorescence loss for these proteins.

claim: IFT20/46/54 re-enter the bb-pool after returning from the cilium.
source: whereas IFT20/46/54 re-enter the bb-pool after returning from the cilium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on FLIP experiments showing significant fluorescence loss for these proteins.

claim: Anterograde IFT trains containing unbleached IFT20/46/54 continued to enter the experimental flagella even after prolonged (>60s) FLIP illumination with a frequency comparable to anterograde IFT in the control flagellum.
source: However, anterograde IFT trains containing unbleached IFT20/46/54 continued to enter the experimental flagella even after prolonged (>60s) FLIP illumination with a frequency comparable to anterograde IFT in the control flagellum (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on prolonged FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The signal strength of anterograde trains in the experimental flagellum during FLIP was generally below those in the control flagellum indicating that these trains contain both bleached proteins derived from retrograde trains and unbleached proteins recruited from the cell body.
source: The signal strength of such trains, however, was generally below those in the control flagellum indicating that these trains contain both bleached proteins derived from retrograde trains and unbleached proteins recruited from the cell body.
evidence: This is based on observations during FLIP experiments with interpretive reasoning.

claim: The signal strength of IFT43-YFP trains exiting the experimental bb-pool under FLIP illumination was ~10% below those in the control flagellum (n = 8).
source: A similar comparison for NG-IFT54 showed a 40% intensity decrease of trains in the experimental flagellum compared to trains in the control flagellum (n = 11; 4–8 measurements per cilium).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of train signal strength during FLIP experiments.

claim: The signal strength of NG-IFT54 trains exiting the experimental bb-pool under FLIP illumination showed a 40% intensity decrease compared to trains in the control flagellum (n = 11).
source: A similar comparison for NG-IFT54 showed a 40% intensity decrease of trains in the experimental flagellum compared to trains in the control flagellum (n = 11; 4–8 measurements per cilium).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of train signal strength during FLIP experiments.

claim: A portion of the IFT-B protein NG-IFT54 in anterograde IFT trains is directly derived from retrograde IFT trains.
source: The data indicate that a portion of the IFT-B protein NG-IFT54 in anterograde IFT trains is directly derived from retrograde IFT trains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 40% intensity decrease observed in FLIP experiments.

claim: C. reinhardtii possess a largely open IFT system, in which proteins are recruited from the cb-pool to the basal bodies, assembled into trains, and travel once through the flagellum before being disassembled and released back into the cell body pool.
source: With the qualification that IFT20/46/54 are partly salvaged, we conclude that C. reinhardtii possess a largely open IFT system, in which proteins are recruited from the cb-pool to the basal bodies, assembled into trains, and travel once through the flagellum before being disassembled and released back into the cell body pool.
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on FLIP experiments.

claim: When FLIP bleaching at one ciliary tip was continued for several minutes the signal of IFT trains progressively diminished in both cilia.
source: When FLIP bleaching at one ciliary tip of a given cell was continued for several minutes the signal of IFT trains progressively diminished in both cilia (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on prolonged FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: After ~6–9 min of FLIP, fluorescent IFT traffic diminished indicating that the entire cellular IFT-FP pool was near exhaustion.
source: After ~6–9 min of FLIP, fluorescent IFT traffic diminished indicating that the entire cellular IFT-FP pool was near exhaustion.
evidence: This is based on prolonged FLIP experiments with interpretive reasoning.

claim: Unbleached NG-IFT54 was evenly distributed between the two flagella.
source: Unbleached NG-IFT54 was evenly distributed between the two flagella.
evidence: This is based on observations during prolonged FLIP experiments.

claim: NG-IFT54 returning to the cb-pool will eventually be reused and bleached and unbleached proteins mix in the cb-pool and are stochastically recruited to the basal body pools.
source: The data suggest that NG-IFT54 returning to the cb-pool will eventually be reused and that bleached and unbleached proteins mix in the cb-pool and are stochastically recruited to the basal body pools.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the even distribution of unbleached NG-IFT54 between flagella.

claim: After bleaching the entire NG-IFT54 population in the experimental flagellum, the signal strength of the experimental bb-pool declined by 52% (STD 8.5%, n = 6) over a period of 5.8 s (STD 0.9 s, n = 6) before reaching a plateau.
source: After the bleaching step, the signal strength of the experimental bb-pool declined by 52% (STD 8.5%, n = 6) over a period of 5.8 s (STD 0.9 s, n = 6) before reaching a plateau (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is based on total flagella FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: ~50% of the NG-IFT54 in the bb-pool is derived from retrograde trains.
source: Thus, ~50% of the NG-IFT54 in the bb-pool is derived from retrograde trains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 52% decline in bb-pool signal after total flagella bleaching.

claim: The first unbleached retrograde train returned after 10.9 s (STD 1.8 s, n = 22) to the experimental basal body after total flagella bleaching.
source: The first unbleached retrograde train returned after 10.9 s (STD 1.8 s, n = 22) to the experimental basal body (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is based on total flagella FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: The bb-pool recovered in strength on average in 16.6 s after the bleaching step (STD 2.4s, n = 6) to levels of the control basal body.
source: Concomitantly with the return of unbleached NG-IFT54 via retrograde traffic, the bb-pool recovered in strength on average in 16.6 s after the bleaching step (STD 2.4s, n = 6) to levels of the control basal body (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is based on total flagella FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: NG-IFT54 entering the bb-pool by retrograde traffic remains for ~6 s in the pool before its release into the cell body or reuse in anterograde trains.
source: The data suggest that NG-IFT54 entering the bb-pool by retrograde traffic remains for ~6 s in the pool before its release into the cell body or reuse in anterograde trains.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the difference between the return time of the first retrograde train (10.9 s) and the recovery time of the bb-pool (16.6 s).

claim: In similar experiments using KAP-GFP or the IFT-A protein IFT43-YFP, the signal strength of the bb-pool attached to the experimental flagellum remained essentially unaltered indicating that these proteins are released into the cb-pool upon return from the cilium.
source: In similar experiments using KAP-GFP or the IFT-A protein IFT43-YFP, the signal strength of the bb-pool attached to the experimental flagellum remained essentially unaltered indicating that these proteins are released into the cb-pool upon return from the cilium (n = 4 and 5, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–H).
evidence: This is based on total flagella FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–H with interpretive reasoning.

claim: After photobleaching of the entire cilium including its bb-pool in IMCD cells, the basal body signal recovered to 60–95% within 16.8 s (STD 7.2 s, n = 11).
source: After photobleaching of the entire cilium including its bb-pool, the basal body signal recovered to 60–95% within 16.8 s (STD 7.2 s, n = 11, normalized using the cilium of a neighboring unbleached cell; Figure 4A,C)
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments in IMCD cells shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: The first unbleached IFT trains entered the cilia of IMCD cells after an average of 18.1 s (STD 9.5 s, n = 39) after photobleaching.
source: the first unbleached IFT trains entered the cilia after an average of 18.1 s (STD 9.5 s, n = 39, Figure 4B; Video 4).
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments in IMCD cells shown in Figure 4B and Video 4.

claim: IFT88-YFP in IMCD cells is continuously recruited from the cell body to the basal bodies and assembled into IFT trains.
source: The data reveal that IFT88-YFP in IMCD cells is continuously recruited from the cell body to the basal bodies and assembled into IFT trains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on FRAP experiments in IMCD cells.

claim: After bleaching of a single cilium with its bb-pool in T. thermophila, the recovery of the basal body signal reached a maximum of 74% (STD 25%, n = 10) of the prebleach value in 29 s (STD 8s, n = 10).
source: After bleaching of a single cilium with its bb-pool, the recovery of the basal body signal became quickly apparent and reached a maximum of 74% (STD 25%, n = 10) of the prebleach value in 29 s (STD 8s, n = 10, Figure 4D–F)
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments in T. thermophila shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: Unbleached anterograde trains were observed in T. thermophila after 17.1 s (STD 8 s, n = 20) after photobleaching.
source: unbleached anterograde trains were observed after 17.1 s (STD 8 s, n = 20; Video 5)
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments in T. thermophila shown in Video 5.

claim: FRAP analysis indicates open and semi-open IFT systems in all three cell types (C. reinhardtii, T. thermophila, and IMCD cells).
source: In summary, FRAP analysis indicates open and semi-open IFT systems in all three cell types.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on FRAP experiments in all three organisms.

claim: The departure of an IFT train resulted in a transient reduction of signal strength at the bb-pool of ~16.1% (STD 7.2%, n = 18) for KAP-GFP, and 12.7% (STD 5.8, n = 20) for NG-IFT54.
source: The departure of an IFT train resulted in a transient reduction of signal strength at the bb-pool of ~16.1% (STD 7.2%, n = 18) for KAP-GFP, and 12.7% (STD 5.8, n = 20) for NG-IFT54 (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of bb-pool signal changes shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: The arrival of a train increased the NG-IFT54 bb-pool signal by up to 25%.
source: Similarly, the arrival of a train increased the NG-IFT54 bb-pool signal by up to 25% (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The amount of IFT protein in the bb-pool is equivalent to a number of IFT trains in the upper single or lower double digits.
source: The data reveal that the departure (or arrival) of a single IFT train appreciably affects the strength of the bb-pool suggesting that the amount of IFT protein in the bb-pool is equivalent to a number of IFT trains in the upper single or lower double digits.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the 12-16% signal change upon train departure/arrival.

claim: NG-IFT54 trains exited the bb-pool at distinct sites resulting in a local depletion of the bb-pool.
source: NG-IFT54 trains, which could be best studied due to their bright and stable signal, exited the bb-pool at distinct sites resulting in a local depletion of the bb-pool (Figure 5D, Video 6).
evidence: This is based on imaging observations shown in Figure 5D and Video 6.

claim: Consecutive trains are often released from distinct sites of the bb-pool.
source: While no particular pattern was observed, the data nevertheless indicate that consecutive trains are often released from distinct sites of the bb-pool.
evidence: This is based on merged kymograms shown in Figure 5E–I.

claim: Bleaching of the bb-pool was followed by an interruption in the traffic of fluorescent anterograde IFT in the experimental flagellum.
source: Typically, bleaching of the bb-pool was followed by an interruption in the traffic of fluorescent anterograde IFT in the experimental flagellum
evidence: This is based on gap analysis experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After the gap anterograde traffic recommenced with prebleach or almost prebleach intensity and frequency.
source: After the gap anterograde traffic recommenced with prebleach or almost prebleach intensity and frequency (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on gap analysis experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The presence of a distinct gap after bleaching of the bb-pool suggests that IFT trains containing the bleached proteins exit the bb-pool before new trains assembled from unbleached proteins emerge.
source: The presence of a distinct gap after bleaching of the bb-pool suggests that IFT trains containing the bleached proteins exit the bb-pool before new trains assembled from unbleached proteins emerge.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gap phenomenon.

claim: The duration of the gap varied considerably for the different IFT proteins analyzed and ranged from ~7 s for IFT140-sfGFP to ~2.5 s for D1bLIC-GFP.
source: The duration of the gap varied considerably for the different IFT proteins analyzed and ranged from ~7 s for IFT140-sfGFP to ~2.5 s for D1bLIC-GFP (Figure 6C; Video 7).
evidence: This is based on gap analysis shown in Figure 6C and Video 7.

claim: The differences in the duration of the gap between each of the two IFT-A, -B1, and -B2 proteins as well as those between the IFT-A and -B2 proteins were not significant.
source: The differences in the duration of the gap between each of the two IFT-A, -B1, and -B2 proteins as well as those between the IFT-A and -B2 proteins were not significant
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gap durations.

claim: The differences in the duration of the gap between IFT-A and -B1 and the motors were significant.
source: while those between IFT-A and -B1 and the motors were.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gap durations.

claim: Distinct IFT proteins need different time spans to transition through the bb-pool from recruitment to release via anterograde IFT.
source: The observation suggests that distinct IFT proteins need different time spans to transition through the bb-pool from recruitment to release via anterograde IFT.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the different gap durations observed for different IFT proteins.

claim: In most experiments (42 of 49), trains labeled only with KAP-GFP reappeared before trains marked by both KAP-GFP and IFT140-mCherry.
source: In most experiments (42 of 49), trains labeled only with KAP-GFP reappeared before trains marked by both KAP-GFP and IFT140-mCherry
evidence: This is based on two-color gap analysis experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the remaining experiments both markers were present in the first postbleach train.
source: in the remaining experiments both markers were present in the first postbleach train (Video 8).
evidence: This is based on two-color gap analysis experiments shown in Video 8.

claim: In the two-color experiments, the average duration of the gaps between bleaching of the bb-pool and the discharge of the first unbleached KAP or IFT140 trains were similar to those determined in the single-tag strains.
source: In the two-color experiments, the average duration of the gaps between bleaching of the bb-pool and the discharge of the first unbleached KAP or IFT140 trains were similar to those determined in the single-tag strains (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of gap durations shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The KAP-GFP signal was restored significantly before that of IFT140-mCherry in two-color FRAP analysis of the bb-pool.
source: The distinct properties of the two proteins were also apparent in two-color FRAP analysis of the bb-pool: The KAP-GFP signal was restored significantly before that of IFT140-mCherry (n = 3, Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is based on two-color FRAP analysis shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: IFT140-sfGFP is recruited early during the assembly of a given IFT train while KAP-GFP is added later.
source: The data indicate that IFT140-sfGFP is recruited early during the assembly of a given IFT train while KAP-GFP is added later (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the two-color gap and FRAP analyses.

claim: In a strain expressing NG-IFT54 (IFT-B1) and IFT140-mCherry (IFT-A), the post-bleach trains mostly contained both fluorescent IFT-proteins (13 of 15 experiments).
source: In a similar analysis using a strain expressing NG-IFT54 (IFT-B1) and IFT140-mCherry (IFT-A), the post-bleach trains mostly contained both fluorescent IFT-proteins (13 of 15 experiments; in two experiments the first train contained NG-IFT54 but not IFT140-mC; not shown).
evidence: This is based on two-color gap analysis experiments.

claim: IFT trains are assembled by sequential addition of distinct IFT proteins/subcomplexes and trains in different states of assembly are lined up in the bb-pool to be successively dispatched into the flagellum upon completion.
source: We propose that IFT trains are assembled by sequential addition of distinct IFT proteins/subcomplexes and that trains in different states of assembly are lined up in the bb-pool to be successively dispatched into the flagellum upon completion.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the gap and FRAP analyses.

claim: sfGFP-tubulin enters cilia with an anterograde frequency of ~20/minute during flagellar regeneration.
source: A prerequisite for this approach is a dense and regular cargo traffic as it has been reported for sfGFP-tubulin, which during flagellar regeneration enters cilia with an anterograde frequency of ~20/minute and even higher frequencies during early regeneration (Craft et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Craft et al., 2015).

claim: The gap between the bleach and the first sfGFP-tubulin trajectory was 1.9 s (STD 1.7 s, n = 25) for the experimental flagellum and 2.1 s (STD 1.6 s, n = 25) for the control flagellum.
source: In detail, the gap between the bleach and the first sfGFP-tubulin trajectory was 1.9 s (STD 1.7 s, n = 25) for the experimental flagellum and 2.1 s (STD 1.6 s, n = 25) for the control flagellum; the difference was not significant (2-tailed t-test p=0.74).
evidence: This is based on gap analysis of sfGFP-tubulin shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: sfGFP-tubulin traffic into the flagella resumed after on average 2.5 s (STD 1.5 s, n = 22) when using an extended laser beam.
source: To ensure proper bleaching of sfGFP-tubulin near the flagellar base, we used an extended laser beam with a diameter of ~2 µm. sfGFP-tubulin traffic into the flagella resumed after on average 2.5 s (STD 1.5 s, n = 22).
evidence: This is based on gap analysis of sfGFP-tubulin shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A similar short gap was observed for D1bLIC, a subunit of IFT dynein, which is transported as a cargo on anterograde trains.
source: Notably, a similar short gap was also observed for D1bLIC, a subunit of IFT dynein, which is transported as a cargo on anterograde trains.
evidence: This is based on gap analysis of D1bLIC-GFP.

claim: sfGFP-tubulin and IFT dynein associate to IFT trains at the flagellar base and briefly before departure into the cilium.
source: Based on these data, we propose that sfGFP-tubulin and IFT dynein associate to IFT trains at the flagellar base and briefly before departure into the cilium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the short gap durations observed for tubulin and D1bLIC.

claim: IFT trains were first observed using DIC microscopy as birefringent particles moving up and down the flagella.
source: IFT trains were first observed using DIC microscopy as birefringent particles moving up and down the flagella (Kozminski et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Kozminski et al., 1993).

claim: Using GFP-tagged proteins, discrete IFT trains traveling inside cilia were observed in various organisms.
source: Using GFP-tagged proteins, discrete IFT trains traveling inside cilia were observed in various organisms (Besschetnova et al., 2009; Mueller et al., 2005; Orozco et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Correlative light-electron microscopy identified IFT trains at as electron opaque arrays with a repetitive ultrastructural moving between the ciliary membrane and the axoneme.
source: Correlative light-electron microscopy identified IFT trains at as electron opaque arrays with a repetitive ultrastructural moving between the ciliary membrane and the axoneme (Kozminski et al., 1995; Stepanek and Pigino, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Kozminski et al., 1995; Stepanek and Pigino, 2016).

claim: The pool of IFT proteins surrounding the basal bodies apparently lacks the well-defined ultrastructure of the trains moving inside cilia.
source: The pool of IFT proteins surrounding the basal bodies apparently lacks the well-defined ultrastructure of the trains moving inside cilia (Rogowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Rogowski et al., 2013).

claim: A closed IFT system was proposed for the IFT-B protein IFT52 in T. brucei.
source: In contrast, a closed IFT system was proposed for the IFT-B protein IFT52 in T. brucei (Buisson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Buisson et al., 2013).

claim: Bleaching of the IFT52-GFP bb-pool in T. brucei was followed by a gap in anterograde traffic and IFT52-GFP from retrograde trains reentered the bb-pool.
source: Similar to our observations on C. reinhardtii IFT-B proteins, bleaching of the IFT52-GFP bb-pool in T. brucei was followed by a gap in anterograde traffic and IFT52-GFP from retrograde trains reentered the bb-pool.
evidence: This is based on findings from Buisson et al., 2013.

claim: When anterograde IFT resumed in T. brucei the signal intensity of the trains was markedly below that of trains prior to the bleaching step and the total recovery of the bb-pool reached only ~50% of the prebleach intensity.
source: However, when anterograde IFT resumed the signal intensity of the trains was markedly below that of trains prior to the bleaching step and the total recovery of the bb-pool reached only ~50% of the prebleach intensity suggesting that the bleached proteins continue to cycle within the flagellum-basal body domain while an exchange with the cb-pool is negligible within the time span of the experiment.
evidence: This is based on findings from Buisson et al., 2013 with interpretive reasoning.

claim: Single molecule imaging showed that kinesin-2 and IFT dynein returning from cilia in C. elegans diffuse briefly near the base to turn around and re-enter the cilium supporting a closed IFT system.
source: Single molecule imaging showed that kinesin-2 and IFT dynein returning from cilia in C. elegans diffuse briefly near the base to turn around and re-enter the cilium supporting a closed IFT system (Mijalkovic et al., 2017; Prevo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Mijalkovic et al., 2017; Prevo et al., 2015).

claim: The bulk of the motor subunits KAP-GFP and D1bLIC-GFP in anterograde trains of C. reinhardtii is recruited from the cb-pool.
source: While our data do not exclude that some motors remain in the basal body-cilium compartment for several rounds of IFT, the bulk of the motor subunits KAP-GFP and D1bLIC-GFP in anterograde trains of C. reinhardtii is recruited from the cb-pool (see Figure 3—figure supplement 3G,H for KAP-GFP).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G,H.

claim: C. elegans cilia possess altered basal bodies and lack the transitional fibers (TFs) in their mature state.
source: In their mature state, C. elegans cilia possess altered basal bodies and lack the transitional fibers (TFs), two structures that are likely to be critical for the recruitment of IFT proteins from the cb-pool to the ciliary base; these changes in could favor a more closed IFT system (Nechipurenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Nechipurenko et al., 2017) with speculative reasoning.

claim: The transitional fibers are likely to be critical for the recruitment of IFT proteins from the cb-pool to the ciliary base.
source: In their mature state, C. elegans cilia possess altered basal bodies and lack the transitional fibers (TFs), two structures that are likely to be critical for the recruitment of IFT proteins from the cb-pool to the ciliary base
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on structural observations.

claim: The bb-pool contains IFT subcomplexes or individual proteins rather than entire IFT particles.
source: It appears that different IFT proteins occupy distinct territories indicating that the bb-pool contains IFT subcomplexes or individual proteins rather than entire IFT particles.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the distinct spatial distributions of different IFT proteins.

claim: The IFT-B protein IFT52 is associated with the TFs.
source: The IFT-B1 protein IFT52 is associated with the TFs
evidence: This is supported by citations (Cole et al., 1998; Deane et al., 2001).

claim: The TFs are required to recruit kinesin-2, but not the IFT particle proteins, into the bb-pool.
source: the TFs are required to recruit kinesin-2, but not the IFT particle proteins, into the bb-pool (Cole et al., 1998; Deane et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Cole et al., 1998; Deane et al., 2001).

claim: The entry of IFT proteins into the cilium depends on kinesin-2.
source: The entry of IFT proteins into the cilium depends on kinesin-2 (Kozminski et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Kozminski et al., 1995).

claim: The binding of kinesin-2 to IFT is regulated by phosphorylation.
source: the binding of kinesin-2 to IFT is regulated by phosphorylation (Liang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Liang et al., 2014).

claim: The addition of kinesin-2 is a late step of train assembly.
source: we show here that the addition of kinesin-2 is a late step of train assembly.
evidence: This is based on the gap analysis data showing short gap durations for KAP-GFP.

claim: The longest average gap in IFT traffic was ~9s for the IFT-A/B2 proteins.
source: The longest average gap in IFT traffic was ~9s for the IFT-A/B2 proteins.
evidence: This is based on gap analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In C. reinhardtii, IFT trains exit the bb-pool with a frequency of ~1/s.
source: In C. reinhardtii, IFT trains exit the bb-pool with a frequency of ~1/s
evidence: This is based on IFT frequency measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: One train is completed each second and ~9 trains in different stages of assembly are in the pool at a given time.
source: In C. reinhardtii, IFT trains exit the bb-pool with a frequency of ~1/s suggesting that one train is completed each second and that ~9 trains in different stages of assembly are in the pool at a given time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ~9s gap duration and ~1/s train frequency.

claim: Each of the nine basal body triplets with its associated structures could assist to assemble one IFT train.
source: In a speculative model, each of the nine basal body triplets with its associated structures could assist to assemble one IFT train.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a speculative model.

claim: The nascent trains move upwards along the triplet blades combining with additional IFT subcomplexes.
source: The nascent trains move upwards along the triplet blades combining with additional IFT subcomplexes.
evidence: This is part of the speculative model proposed.

claim: Nascent trains associate with kinesin-2 at the TFs, which will pull the nascent train upwards and into the cilium, compressing and concentrating the IFT material between the microtubules and the membrane.
source: Then, they will associate with kinesin-2 at the TFs, which will pull the nascent train upwards and into the cilium, compressing and concentrating the IFT material between the microtubules and the membrane.
evidence: This is part of the speculative model proposed.

claim: Once a position is vacated by a departing train, the assembly of a new train is initiated near the proximal end of the basal body.
source: Once a position is vacated by a departing train, the assembly of a new train is initiated near the proximal end of the basal body (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is part of the speculative model proposed and illustrated in Figure 8F.

claim: The CH domain of IFT81 and the N-terminal domain of IFT74 bind tubulin in vitro.
source: The calponin-homology (CH) domain of IFT81 and the N-terminal domain of IFT74 bind tubulin in vitro
evidence: This is supported by citations (Bhogaraju et al., 2013; Kubo et al., 2016; Taschner et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017b).

claim: Cilia assembly is impaired in C. reinhardtii strains carrying mutations in both the CH domain of IFT81 and the N-terminal domain of IFT74.
source: cilia assembly is impaired in C. reinhardtii strains carrying mutations in both domains indicating that the IFT81/74 module is the dominant tubulin binding site of IFT (Bhogaraju et al., 2013; Kubo et al., 2016; Taschner et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations with interpretive reasoning.

claim: The IFT81/74 module is the dominant tubulin binding site of IFT.
source: indicating that the IFT81/74 module is the dominant tubulin binding site of IFT (Bhogaraju et al., 2013; Kubo et al., 2016; Taschner et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: IFT81 and IFT74 are core structural components of the IFT-B1 complex.
source: IFT81 and IFT74 are core structural components of the IFT-B1 complex (Lucker et al., 2005; Taschner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Lucker et al., 2005; Taschner et al., 2014).

claim: Tubulin loading occurs in the basal bodies pool and briefly before the trains move into the cilium.
source: The data indicate that tubulin loading occurs in the basal bodies pool and briefly before the trains move into the cilium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the short gap duration for sfGFP-tubulin.

claim: Axonemal cargoes are mostly released from IFT trains at the ciliary tip where IFT trains partially disassemble to reorganize for retrograde traffic.
source: Axonemal cargoes are mostly released from IFT trains at the ciliary tip where IFT trains partially disassemble to reorganize for retrograde traffic (Bower et al., 2013; Craft et al., 2015; Johnson and Rosenbaum, 1992; Lechtreck et al., 2013b; Wren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cargo binding and unloading could be linked to train assembly and disassembly.
source: We speculate that cargo binding and unloading could be linked to train assembly and disassembly.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: C. elegans mutants in the TF protein Dyf-19 have severely reduced amounts of IFT proteins and IFT traffic inside cilia.
source: C. elegans mutants in the TF protein Dyf-19 have severely reduced amounts of IFT proteins and IFT traffic inside cilia (Wei et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Wei et al., 2013).

claim: Anterograde traffic results in trajectories running from the bottom left to the top right in kymograms.
source: Anterograde traffic results in trajectories running from the bottom left to the top right
evidence: This describes how to interpret kymograms.

claim: Retrograde traffic is presented by lines running from the top left to the bottom right in kymograms.
source: retrograde traffic is presented by lines running from the top left to the bottom right.
evidence: This describes how to interpret kymograms.
